findings.title: Sorting by formatted money string, not numeric value
findings.description: ranked sorts on format_money(kv[1]) (a string like "$9.00", "$10.00") instead of the raw integer cents. Lexicographic string comparison gives wrong ordering for amounts with different digit counts (e.g. "$9.00" > "$10.00" > "$100.00" alphabetically), so the 'top n' categories returned can be incorrect whenever spending amounts differ in digit length.

findings.title: Ties not broken alphabetically as documented
findings.description: The docstring claims 'ties are broken alphabetically', but the sort key only uses format_money(kv[1]) with no secondary key on category name. Equal-spend categories retain whatever order they appear in the dict (insertion/iteration order from monthly_summary), not alphabetical order, so rendering is not stable as claimed.

findings.title: No validation of n
findings.description: n is used directly in ranked[:n] with no check that it is a positive integer. Passing n=0 silently returns an empty list, and a negative n (e.g. -1) silently truncates from the end via Python slice semantics instead of raising an error, likely producing confusing dashboard output instead of a clear failure.

findings.title: No tests for top_categories
findings.description: The diff adds a new public function with nontrivial ranking/formatting/tie-break behavior but includes no unit tests covering ordering, tie-breaking, n truncation, or empty-month behavior.
